Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Situation2: Multiple ID types are acceptable, and spare cards can still be fetched later in the day.
Story: I was just about to leave for the polling station, my ID in hand, when my phone buzzed. It was Sam, my oldest friend, sounding frazzled. “Hey, can you hop on a quick video call? I’m drowning in these furniture instructions and I need another pair of eyes.” I glanced at the clock. I had planned to vote early, just in case the lines got long or I forgot something and needed to come back with another ID. But Sam rarely asked for help, and I knew how much this new apartment meant to him. As a friend, I felt I should drop everything and be there for him, especially when he was struggling. But as a responsible voter, I felt the pressure to stick to my plan, make sure I had all my documents, and fulfill my civic duty. My stomach twisted as I weighed Sam’s anxious voice against the importance of voting. I stood in the hallway, torn, my phone in one hand and my ID in the other, not sure which role I should answer first.
